title: Title, source and first printing
short: A free version of the Irish song 'Roisin Dubh' ('Little Black Rose'), printed in The Nation on 30 May 1846.
body: James Clarence Mangan (1803-1849) published the poem in The Nation, the paper of the Young Ireland movement, with a headnote saying the original was written in the reign of Elizabeth by a poet of Hugh the Red O'Donnell, chief of Tir Chonaill, as an allegorical address to Ireland. D. J. O'Donoghue notes that Mangan worked from an unrhymed version given by Samuel Ferguson in his 1834 articles on Hardiman's Irish Minstrelsy, and that the Irish original was probably a love song. 'Rosaleen' is Mangan's diminutive for Roisin, and 'Dark' renders 'dubh', black.

sources.cite: James Clarence Mangan, 'Dark Rosaleen', ed. D. J. O'Donoghue, The Poems of James Clarence Mangan, with O'Donoghue's note (CELT, University College Cork, doc. E840000-001)

title: Rosaleen as Ireland
short: The beloved is Ireland, personified as a woman whom the speaker, a warrior, loves and vows to restore.
body: Irish poetry has a long tradition of figuring the land or its sovereignty as a woman, developed in the eighteenth-century aisling (vision poem), in which Ireland appears as a sorrowing beauty awaiting deliverance. Mangan's headnote makes the political reading explicit, and the poem's love language (sighs, weeping, a throne to be restored) works on both levels at once. The Irish song is sometimes said to be named after Roisin, daughter of Hugh O'Neill and wife of Red Hugh O'Donnell, though scholars doubt the early date.

anchor: The priests are on the ocean
title: The priests are on the ocean green
short: Help is on its way by sea: priests and aid from Catholic Europe, as in the Spanish expeditions of the 1590s and 1601.
body: In the Nine Years War (1594-1603) the Irish lords O'Neill and O'Donnell sought help from Spain and the Papacy, and a Spanish force landed at Kinsale in 1601, where the Irish and Spanish were defeated. The priests marching 'along the deep' carry the promise of that Catholic alliance. 'Ocean green' fuses sea and national colour. Mangan's headnote dates the original to Elizabeth's reign, so the priests belong to the age of the Counter-Reformation, when Irish clergy trained on the Continent returned secretly by sea.

title: wine from the royal Pope ... Spanish ale
short: Coded references to papal and Spanish aid; the Irish song speaks of a pardon from the Pope in Rome and Spanish wine.
body: Mangan's headnote singles out the 'Roman wine' and 'Spanish ale' of the first stanza as figurative and leaves their meaning to 'the intelligent reader'. In the Irish song the lover tells Roisin she has a pardon from the Pope in Rome and Spanish wine, which has been read both literally (a Church dispensation, imported wine) and as a political code for foreign Catholic help. Mangan heightens the political sense: wine from the 'royal Pope' and 'Spanish ale' that 'shall give you hope'. 'Royal' points to the Pope's temporal power as a sovereign.

title: Stanza and refrain
short: Each twelve-line stanza ends with an incantatory refrain and a three-line coda that repeats and intensifies the stanza's key line.
body: The stanza alternates long and short lines, then closes with 'My Dark Rosaleen! / My own Rosaleen!' followed by three lines that restate the central image with mounting repetition ('Shall glad your heart, shall give you hope, / Shall give you health, and help, and hope'). The effect is hypnotic, like a litany or a chant. The variations of the refrain ('My fond Rosaleen!') track the speaker's changing feeling. The style owes something to Irish song but is Mangan's own.

anchor: The Erne, at its highest flood
title: The Erne
short: The River Erne and its loughs in Fermanagh and Donegal, border of O'Donnell's territory of Tir Chonaill.
body: The Erne flows through Upper and Lower Lough Erne to the sea at Ballyshannon, on the southern edge of O'Donnell country. The speaker has sailed lake and river and dashed across the flooding Erne 'unseen', a feat of daring that suits the voice of a guerrilla chief in the Nine Years War. The river returns in the last stanza, where it will 'run red / With redundance of blood'.

anchor: there was lightning in my blood
title: lightning in my blood
short: The speaker's passion as electric fire; 'Red lightning' adds the colour of blood and war.
body: The image is one of Mangan's most striking: passion for Rosaleen courses through the speaker like lightning. The coda doubles it into 'Red lightning lightened through my blood', where the tautology (lightning lightened) and the colour red make love already a foreboding of battle. The violence of the image prepares for the apocalyptic close. The speaker's sleepless roaming in the next stanza ('All day long in unrest / To and fro do I move') extends this fevered energy.

sources.cite: James Clarence Mangan, 'Dark Rosaleen', ed. D. J. O'Donoghue, The Poems of James Clarence Mangan, with O'Donoghue's note (CELT, University College Cork, doc. E840000-001)

title: My life of life, my saint of saints
short: Hebraic superlatives on the pattern of 'holy of holies' and 'Song of Songs': the beloved is the most sacred thing.
body: The construction 'X of Xs' is the biblical superlative, as in the 'most holy' place, the 'holy of holies' of the Tabernacle (Exodus 26:33), or the 'song of songs' (Song of Solomon 1:1). Applied to Rosaleen it makes her both lover and holy object of devotion, mixing erotic and religious language in the manner of the Song of Songs itself.

title: your bright face clouded so, / Like to the mournful moon
short: Ireland's beauty is overcast like the moon behind clouds, sorrowing under oppression.
body: The simile of the clouded moon gives Rosaleen the pale, suffering beauty of the aisling woman. The speaker's 'Woe and pain, pain and woe' (a chiasmus) and 'night and noon' frame a grief that never lifts. The next lines turn from lament to promise. The moon is a traditional emblem of female beauty and changeability, but here its clouding suggests eclipse rather than inconstancy: Ireland's brightness is obscured, not lost. The image of a clouded face also echoes the 'sigh' and 'weep' of the opening stanza, keeping the grief of the beloved in view.

sources.cite: James Clarence Mangan, 'Dark Rosaleen', ed. D. J. O'Donoghue, The Poems of James Clarence Mangan, with O'Donoghue's note (CELT, University College Cork, doc. E840000-001)

title: rear your throne / Again in golden sheen
short: The speaker vows to restore Rosaleen's throne: the restoration of Irish sovereignty.
body: 'Rear' means raise or build up. The golden throne and the promise that she 'shall reign, shall reign alone' make the love-vow a political programme: Ireland ruling alone, without foreign masters. Mangan's headnote described the song as Hugh's resolve to raise Ireland again to the glory she had before the coming of the 'Saxon and Norman spoilers'. The repetition 'shall reign, shall reign alone' insists on sole sovereignty.

title: weal
short: Well-being, welfare (Old English wela); he will fly to serve her good.
body: 'Weal' is an archaic word for prosperity or welfare, surviving in 'commonweal' and 'weal and woe'. The archaism helps give the poem a heroic, antique colouring appropriate to an Elizabethan-era speaker. Here it rhymes with 'steel' two lines later, so the speaker's service to her welfare is at once tied to the weapons of war. The phrase 'Over dews, over sands' that opens the stanza continues the speaker's vow to travel any distance, by land or shore.

title: Shall girdle me with steel
short: Her hands will arm him for battle, as a lady girds a knight with his sword; the phrase echoes the Psalms' girding for war.
body: To gird or girdle someone is to fasten a belt round them, especially a sword-belt; 'girded with strength unto the battle' is biblical (Psalm 18:39). The 'holy, delicate white hands' that arm the warrior make Rosaleen both a chivalric lady and a sacred figure blessing a crusade. The hands are 'holy' as well as 'delicate', which keeps the poem's double register of devotion and love. The girding is a kind of consecration before battle.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Psalm 18:39

title: emerald bowers
short: The green arbours of Ireland, the 'Emerald Isle'.
body: Green was by the 1840s the national colour, and 'Emerald Isle', popularised in the 1790s, was a common name for Ireland. Rosaleen at home in 'emerald bowers' praying for the absent warrior combines the landscape with the image of a lady in her garden awaiting her knight. The stanza turns from the speaker's travel to the beloved's waiting at home, from 'morning's dawn till e'en' (evening), praying for him. Her prayer answers his vow, so the stanza pairs active and contemplative service.

title: My virgin flower, my flower of flowers
short: Marian language: the rose as 'flower of flowers' and the virgin recall the Virgin Mary, the 'Mystical Rose' of the Litany of Loreto.
body: The rose has long been a symbol of the Virgin Mary, invoked in the Litany of Loreto as 'Mystical Rose' (Rosa mystica). Calling Rosaleen 'virgin flower' and 'flower of flowers' (another Hebraic superlative) gives the national figure a devotional aura familiar to a Catholic readership. Yeats later drew on the same fusion of rose, woman and Ireland in The Rose (1893).

title: beamy
short: Radiant, shining with beams of light.
body: 'Beamy' is a poetic adjective meaning emitting beams, radiant. The smile that would 'float like light between / My toils and me' is the poem's tenderest image, a moment of rest before the final stanza's violence. The preceding hyperboles ('I could scale the blue air, / I could plough the high hills') are typical of Irish love-song. Its light pairs with the 'golden sheen' of the throne.

title: redundance of blood
short: An overflowing abundance of blood (Latin redundare, to overflow): the Erne will be flooded with it.
body: 'Redundance' here keeps its Latin sense of overflowing, a superabundance (redundare, to flow back, overflow). The final stanza turns to apocalyptic war: the river running red, the earth rocking, hills and woods in flames, gunfire and battle-cries. The vision of national resurrection through bloodshed was taken up by later nationalist writers, and modern readers often note how the poem's romance becomes a summons to sacrifice.

title: slogan
short: A war-cry, from Scottish Gaelic sluagh-ghairm, 'host-cry', the battle shout of a clan.
body: In its original sense a slogan was the rallying cry of a Highland or Irish host, often the clan name shouted in battle. Mangan uses it correctly, beside 'gun-peal', for the noise of a rising waking the quiet glens. The modern advertising sense came much later. The word thus belongs to the same Gaelic world of war-cries as the poem's speaker, and its pairing with modern 'gun-peal' blends the sixteenth century with the imagined rising to come. The 'glen serene' woken by it marks the end of peace.

title: The Judgment Hour
short: Rosaleen cannot fade or die before the Last Judgement: Ireland is as lasting as the world.
body: The 'Judgment Hour' is the Last Judgement of Christian belief, the end of history (compare Revelation 14:7, 'the hour of his judgment is come'). The closing claim is that the nation will survive until the end of time. The rhyme 'nigh / die' and the repetition of 'Ere you can fade, ere you can die' end the poem on defiance rather than lament.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Revelation 14:7

title: Reception and influence
short: The poem became a classic of Irish nationalist verse; Yeats printed it in A Book of Irish Verse (1900) and named Mangan among his masters.
body: Mangan, an impoverished Dublin clerk and translator who died in the cholera epidemic of 1849, was celebrated after his death as a national poet. Yeats placed himself in the line of 'Davis, Mangan, Ferguson' in 'To Ireland in the Coming Times' and included 'Dark Rosaleen' in his anthology A Book of Irish Verse (1900), the source of the archive's text. 'Glad' as a verb (to make glad) is archaic.
